newsitem.title: UK: Ten years on the Louvre Accord belongs in a museum.
newsitem.headline: Ten years on the Louvre Accord belongs in a museum.

text.p: Ten years to the month after it was hailed as a major triumph of international financial cooperation, the Paris Louvre Accord now has the air of an exhibit in the museum which gave it its name.
Looking back at the agreement to stabilise the dollar after a dramatic fall from dizzy heights, even its main protagonists cannot agree now on whether it was a success.
The deal was sealed on an icy cold February 22 in 1987 in the Louvre Palace in Paris which then housed the French Finance Ministry as well as France's most famous art gallery.
Finance ministers and central bank governors from the major industrial nations had decided that the dollar's decline since 1985 had gone far enough and they wanted stability.
But the deal made an inauspicious start more reminiscent of a French farce than a major breakthrough of international financial diplomacy.
The Italian delegation, led by the late Italian politician Giovanni Goria, stormed home in a fit of pique.

The Italians were angry at being asked -- along with Canada -- effectively to rubber-stamp a deal which had been worked out already by the powerful Group of Five (G5) nations -- the United States, Japan, Germany, France and Britain.
Canada stayed to produce a "G6" accord which was in the end also endorsed by Italy and the G7 process of economic coordination and cooperation was finally deemed to be in place.

The agreement did usher in a period of calm on the markets after officials pledged "to cooperate closely (codeword for currency market intervention) to foster stability of exchange rates around current levels".
But that spirit of cooperation was in tatters only months later when a row erupted between U.S. Treasury Secretary James Baker and the German Bundesbank about the level of German interest rates.
The very public dispute upset market confidence and helped trigger the global stock market meltdown in October that year.
Nigel Lawson, British finance minister at the time, says the Louvre Accord worked reasonably well for a period.

But in his memoirs he adds, "The weakness of the accord, which eventually undermined it, was its failure to bolster the pledge to intervene in the foreign exchange markets with an undertaking to adjust domestic monetary policies to validate the agreed (currency) ranges".

Japan's Deputy Finance Minister in 1987, Toyoo Gyoten, is just as forthright. Asked this month by Reuters Financial Television whether the G7 had reached its objectives in Paris, he answered, "No -- I don't think we did."

The G7 had tried to stabilise exchange rates around current levels. "But we were not sure whether the current rate was the rate which markets accepted as a stable and sustainable level. That was our major mistake," Gyoten said.
Baker's deputy of the time, David Mulford, disputes that the deal was a failure, describing the accord as "not perfect" but a "significant achievement".

Baker's German counterpart in the 1980s, Gerhard Stoltenberg, told Reuters Louvre was viewed more critically than the 1985 Plaza Accord, when the G5 successfully agreed to bring the dollar lower because its strength was producing severe global economic imbalances.
But he sides more with Mulford, saying, "With certain reservations I would call Louvre a success."
Ten years after the Louvre deal, the sheer size of the global financial markets has rendered grand schemes to direct currencies more or less obsolete.
This month's meeting of G7 finance ministers in Berlin also had the objective of stabilising the dollar -- after its recent relentless rise against both the yen and the mark.
But those talks in the German capital never appeared likely to produce a "Berlin Accord".

Markets doubted that any nation other than Japan really wanted to do much about the strong dollar, which is keeping inflation down in the United States and helping exports in an economically depressed continental Europe.
Perhaps more importantly the ministers also revealed that there had been no suggestion in Berlin that central banks would intervene to adjust the dollar's level.

With between one and two trillion dollars being exchanged every day on the foreign currency markets now, there is a growing doubt whether intervention -- an important cornerstone of Louvre -- can work for anything but the very short term.
